title: Oracle files to sell $20B in new stock, bonds to finance AI buildout
content:
Oracle filed plans on Monday to issue new stock and more debt to finance its artificial intelligence buildout.
The hyperscaler will sell $10 billion in common stock and $10 billion in senior notes, according to filings with the Securities and Exchange Commission. While the fundraising was already outlined at an investor day last week, shares tumbled 8.8% Monday.
"This seems to be exactly what they previewed," said Rob Oliver, senior research analyst at Baird. "So I'm not sure why the market is freaking about it."
Oracle said it plans to use the proceeds for general corporate purposes, which may include capital expenditures, repayments of debt and future investments.
The hyperscaler's stock initially bounced after last Wednesday's investor day, when Oracle also issued a revenue forecast of at least $225 billion for fiscal 2030. At the time Oracle also said it was limiting its additional capital market funding for the fiscal 2027 to 2030 investment cycle to that $20 billion.
"This is a major relief given concerns about the state of debt markets and the cost of capital (although UBS has argued that these debt market concerns have been over-stated)," UBS analyst Karl Keirstead said in a note on Thursday.
Oracle plans to turn to vendor financing, customer-provided hardware and customer prepayments to help it transition to positive free cash flow, which it expects to reach in the second half of 2028.
Stock and bonds in Oracle, co-founded by former CEO Larry Ellison, have been under pressure amid growing investor concerns about the massive amount of debt being taken on to fund AI infrastructure.
Oracle shares are down 33% in 2026 and 50% over the past 12 months. The yield on its investment-grade 4.95% bond due in 2031 is currently 7.276%.
The sentiment shift is also seen in Oracle's five-year credit default swaps, which are insurance against default. The spread sits at 292, up 265% in one year. That's more in line with a high-end junk bond rating, according to S&P Global Market Intelligence's Gavan Nolan.
While still an investment-grade credit, Oracle was downgraded by S&P to a BBB- in July, one rating level above high yield. It has $125.34 billion in debt, as of Aug. 31, with the bulk in senior notes.
What ultimately matters for Oracle is execution, Pat Nerney, head of investment solutions at Dynasty Financial Partners, said in an email to CNBC Monday.
"Can they do what they say they are going to do? We view this as the narrative across the AI space," he said. "If this gets executed according to plans laid out, they will be rewarded. If they have to come back to market in the back half of '27 after telling everyone this was the last of the capital needed ... look out."
— CNBC's Seema Mody and Ari Levy contributed reporting.

report.summary: Oracle filed to raise $20B via $10B stock and $10B senior notes to fund AI infrastructure, as investors worry about debt and execution.
report.background: Oracle has become a major AI infrastructure provider, but its buildout requires enormous capital. At its investor day last week, Oracle forecast at least $225 billion in revenue for fiscal 2030 and said it would cap additional capital-market funding for the fiscal 2027-2030 investment cycle at $20 billion. That framing was meant to reassure investors worried about AI-related debt. Still, Oracle carries $125.34 billion in debt as of Aug. 31, was downgraded by S&P to BBB- in July, and its five-year credit default swaps have jumped to levels more typical of junk bonds. Its shares are down 33% in 2026 and 50% over 12 months, reflecting broad anxiety about how hyperscalers will finance AI data centers.
key_points: Oracle filed with the SEC to sell $10 billion in common stock and $10 billion in senior notes. The company said proceeds will go toward general corporate purposes, which may include capital expenditures, debt repayment and future investments. The fundraising was already previewed at investor day, so the filing formalizes a plan rather than announcing a surprise.

Despite the preview, Oracle shares fell 8.8% on Monday. Baird analyst Rob Oliver said the market reaction was puzzling because the plan was exactly what Oracle had outlined. The drop suggests investors are highly sensitive to any signal that AI infrastructure spending will require more external financing.

Credit markets are flashing caution. Oracle has $125.34 billion in debt, a BBB- rating from S&P, and a 2031 bond yielding 7.276%. Its five-year credit default swap spread sits at 292, up 265% in a year, which S&P Global Market Intelligence's Gavan Nolan said is more in line with a high-end junk rating.

Oracle expects to reach positive free cash flow in the second half of 2028, aided by vendor financing, customer-provided hardware and customer prepayments. Analysts say execution is the key test: if Oracle delivers, it will be rewarded; if it returns to capital markets after calling this the last needed funding, confidence could suffer badly.

The company also issued a fiscal 2030 revenue forecast of at least $225 billion and limited additional capital-market funding for the 2027-2030 investment cycle to $20 billion. UBS called that cap a relief given debt-market concerns. However, the gap between forecast ambition and current credit strain remains the central investor debate.
report.impact: For the AI industry, Oracle's move highlights a shift from cash-funded AI capex to debt- and equity-funded expansion. If investors demand higher returns, other hyperscalers and AI startups may face tougher financing and greater scrutiny of data-center spending. For developers, compute supply may keep growing, but access and pricing could depend on Oracle's execution and customer prepayment models. For regular users, AI services may continue to improve, yet higher capital costs could eventually feed into subscription prices or slower feature rollout. The biggest risk is a confidence shock if Oracle or peers stumble, which could ripple across cloud contracts, chip demand and the broader AI trade.
report.tools: To follow the financing story, use SEC EDGAR full-text search for Oracle's S-3, 8-K and bond filings; OpenBB or yfinance for equity and bond data; and FRED for rates and credit conditions. Track CDS and ratings commentary via S&P Global Market Intelligence and analyst notes. For AI infrastructure context, follow SemiAnalysis, The Information and CNBC tech. Open-source finance dashboards such as OpenBB let you monitor Oracle's stock, debt and peer comparisons in one place.
